newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK-China border ready for historic troop crossing.
newsitem.headline: HK-China border ready for historic troop crossing.

text.p: The sendoff will be emotional, the welcome uncertain.

When Chinese combat troops enter Hong Kong on June 30, their first glimpse of the territory will be a bleak border post flanked by truck and container parks where the air is thick with mosquitoes and diesel fumes.
The People's Liberation Army (PLA) is sending 509 soldiers into Hong Kong at 9 p.m. on June 30 to take up positions ahead of the territory's midnight handover from Britain to China.
The troops are expected to travel from the Chinese boom town of Shenzhen into Hong Kong along a limited-access highway which looks and smells like the New Jersey turnpike outside New York city.
However drab the setting, though, the border crossing by Chinese troops will be historic after Britain's colonial interlude of 156 years.
The huge volume of truck traffic using the route leaves little doubt that, whatever their political status, southern China and Hong Kong have been economically merged for years.
A drive down Shenzhen's main street on Tuesday evening revealed a city dressing up for Monday's historic handover. Red paper lanterns lined the busy highway, dancing in the breeze.
Workers scrambled in the darkness to hang decorations at the Chinese customs post on the edge of town.
Riding on the back of Hong Kong's spectacular success, the Shenzhen special economic zone has grown from a fishing and farming village to a bustling city of three million in only a generation.
Gleaming office towers spike the sky and building sites are scattered everywhere.

But residents seem more preoccupied with the vagaries of the local stock market than they do with the handover, which they have been hearing about since 1984 when Britain agreed to surrender Hong Kong.
Asked his thoughts about Hong Kong's return to China, one stock analyst in Shenzhen mentioned only that he was looking forward to the holiday time off.
Hong Kong customs officials at the border squirmed and refused to answer when asked if they would be checking the papers and gear of PLA soldiers on the night of the handover.

PLA troops coming across in the hours before midnight have been authorised to bring in pistols and rifles, packed in cases, which they will take to barracks being abandoned by departing British troops.
Hong Kong police on a hilltop overlooking the border remain focused on their nightly vigil of guarding against illegal immigrants.
Under the "one country, two systems" policy the border will remain in place after the handover and Hong Kong will be preserved as a distinct entity for 50 years.
